results.content: Why multiple hypothesis test corrections provide poor control of false positives in the real world Stanley E. These three p-values are rarely corrected for multiple testing [15], but they are a family of related tests since they use the same data, are part of the same statistical model, and use the same error term when calculating the p-values. It is rare for all the tests that relate to a research question to be grouped as a family, but it is a sensible way to control error rates. A more stringent approach is to adjust all the p-values reported in a paper, such that the probability of at least one false positive amongst all the reported hypothesis tests is 0.05. Many MCPs work in a similar way; a new cutoff is calculated from the number of tests (or the p-value adjusted), but the details vary for each method. 5 Freedom to choose the correction method After deciding the family of tests and the error rate, researchers have (too) many options for the method of correction: for the FWER, options include Bonferroni [9], progressive Bonferroni [35], Holm [36], Scheffe [64], Sidak [67], Tukey [78], Student-Newman-Keuls [41, 54], Dunn [22], Duncan [21], Dunnett [23] and so on; and for the FDR, options include Benjamini-Hochberg [4], Benjamini-Yekutieli [5], Q-value [72, 73], local FDR, positive FDR [72, 73] marginal FDR [77], conditional FDR [77], empirical FDR [77], Black Box FDR [74], Beta-Uniform mixture [59], and so on. Dozens of methods exist to correct for multiple comparisons and researchers are free to choose (subject to restrictions on the type of comparison), sometimes making their selection based on the results, and choosing the method that provides signiﬁcant p-values for the key comparisons. Even if each research group carefully controls the FPR, the same data is analysed in so many ways by so many people that every false positive result will likely be found and reported. Sometimes the SD is underestimated so that even a small effect size can lead to a large test statistic and hence a signiﬁcant p-value. First, many error rates exist – per-comparison, familywise, false dis-covery, and per-family – so by deﬁnition there cannot be a generic “false positive rate” that a researcher can control.

results.title: Multiple test correction: Bonferroni, FDR | ABI Bioinformatics Guide 2024
results.content: # Multiple test correction: Bonferroni, FDR. Multiple test correction methods are used to control the increased risk of Type I errors (false positives) when performing multiple statistical tests simultaneously. Multiple testing corrections adjust p-values derived from multiple statistical tests to correct for occurrence of false positives. ### The Bonferroni correction. The Bonferroni correction is a straightforward and conservative approach that adjusts the significance level by dividing it by the number of tests performed. This reduces the likelihood of false positives but can also increase the risk of Type II errors (false negatives) due to its stringent nature. ### The False Discovery Rate. The False Discovery Rate (FDR) method, such as the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, is a less conservative approach that controls the expected proportion of false positives among the rejected hypotheses. FDR methods are more powerful than the Bonferroni correction, allowing for the identification of more true positives while still controlling for false discoveries.

results.title: How to use Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing
results.content: For instance, if you're running 20 tests with a significance level of 0.05, there's a whopping 64% chance of seeing at least one false positive without any correction. By adjusting our significance level using methods like the Bonferroni correction, we can keep the FWER at the desired level. Enter the Bonferroni correction—a simple yet powerful tool to adjust significance levels and reduce the risk of false positives in multiple comparisons. This gives you the **Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold** (α/m), ensuring the family-wise error rate (FWER) stays controlled at your desired level. Just divide your desired significance level (α) by the number of comparisons to get the Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold. By adjusting p-values for multiple comparisons, you can make more informed decisions based on reliable statistical evidence—avoiding the pitfalls of false positives. By allowing a small proportion of false positives, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure is less conservative than the Bonferroni correction and more powerful in detecting true positives.

results.title: Sage Research Methods - The SAGE Encyclopedia of Communication Research Methods - Bonferroni Correction
results.content: * **In:**The SAGE Encyclopedia of Communication Research Methods. The Bonferroni correction is a method for adjusting alpha (α) across a set of significance tests where α is the probability of making a Type I error. For a single significance test, a researcher sets an α-level representing the risk the researcher will reject the null hypotheses when the null is true. If α is set at p < .05 then there is a 5% chance for that test the researcher will reject the null hypothesis when within the population the null hypothesis is in fact true. If we consider the aforementioned α of p < .05, then for every 20 tests conducted it is likely at least one of those tests will produce a Type I error. Thus, the more tests a researcher conducts, the more the researchers may capitalize on chance and identify a significant effect when in fact no such effect exists with a population. While α is the chance of making a Type I error on a single statistical test, the term αew is used to express experiment-wise error rate (also called familywise error rate). If each statistical test is evaluated at the same α, the experimentwise error rate or αew is calculated as follows:. The Bonferroni correction was developed in order to adjust αew for a collection of tests to align with the α-level the researcher set for the study. If a researcher has selected an experiment-wise error rate of p < .05, and the study contains 5 hypothesis tests, an experimenter using Bonferroni corrections should consider α = .05/5 or p < .01 for each individual test. The researcher would first calculate a Bonferroni correction for three tests (α/c = .017). Given this result the researcher would fail to reject the null hypothesis for the first test where p = .02. Thus, following the sequential procedure the researcher recalculates the Bonferroni correction for two hypotheses (α/c = .025). The remaining α-levels are below this cutoff and thus would be retained in the sequential procedure, whereas using a standard Bonferroni correction only one test would be retained.
